paragraphs: This paper tackles pathfinding in graphs so large that directly exploring their states is impractical. Its approach combines a neural network that estimates diffusion distance with beam search. The learned distance guides the search, while beam search maintains a limited collection of promising candidate paths. Rubik’s cubes provide a demanding test of this combination.

For 4×4×4 and 5×5×5 cubes, the authors report shorter solutions than all available solvers, including improvements on every case in the combined best results from the Kaggle Santa 2023 challenge. For 3×3×3 cubes, the method finds optimal solutions in more than 98% of cases, compared with the reported 60.3% for DeepCubeA and 69.6% for EfficientCube.

The current implementation also solves 3×3×3 cubes approximately 25.6 times faster and needs up to 8.5 times less training time than the most efficient competing method. Beyond cubes, a single trained agent solves diverse puzzles represented by Cayley graphs containing up to 10^145 states. These findings support the method’s applicability across the evaluated puzzle families.
neurips-2025-a-machine-learning-approach.tldr: A learned distance estimator combined with beam search produces unusually short Rubik’s cube solutions and solves other enormous graph-based puzzles.

paragraphs: BEAST represents action sequences using B-splines, encoding them into compact tokens that can be either discrete or continuous. This gives imitation-learning models a structured way to generate sequences of control actions. The B-spline formulation ensures smooth trajectories, including continuity where adjacent trajectory segments meet, making smoothness part of the representation itself.

Unlike action tokenizers based on vector quantization or byte pair encoding, BEAST does not require a separate tokenizer-training stage. It also produces tokens of uniform length, supporting fast parallel decoding. The authors integrate it with three different architectures: a variational autoencoder, a decoder-only Transformer, and the pretrained Florence-2 vision-language model. These integrations test its compatibility with different token types and model designs.

Evaluation covers 166 simulated tasks across three benchmarks, plus eight real-world tasks across three robot settings. The reported results show substantially lower training and inference costs, smooth high-frequency control signals, and competitive task success rates. The contribution therefore combines computational efficiency with a trajectory representation suited to continuous control.
neurips-2025-beast-efficient-tokenizatio.tldr: BEAST uses B-splines to encode smooth action sequences efficiently, reducing computation while maintaining competitive success across simulated and real robot tasks.

paragraphs: When several predictive models form an ensemble, uncertainty estimates must account for their combined predictions. Conformal prediction provides prediction regions without assuming a particular distributional form. Existing aggregation methods merge the regions produced by individual models, seeking to preserve coverage guarantees while avoiding regions that are unnecessarily broad.

This paper argues that combining those final regions discards useful structure in the underlying conformal scores. Its framework instead extends the usual single-valued score to a multivariate score. Keeping multiple score components available gives the aggregation method more information to work with before constructing a prediction region. The aim is greater efficiency in the uncertainty estimate: less conservative regions.

The authors apply the framework to classification and to regression settings where predictions feed into a subsequent optimization problem. They report empirical advantages over alternative conformal aggregation methods in these settings. The central contribution is a change in where aggregation happens, preserving score-level structure that can help produce more informative ensemble uncertainty estimates.
neurips-2025-conformal-prediction-for-en.tldr: Aggregating multivariate conformal scores preserves information that can make ensemble prediction regions less conservative.

paragraphs: This paper examines whether prompting reasoning models to continue thinking actually improves their answers. Across the studied models and benchmarks, extending reasoning initially improves performance, but further extension leads to a decline. The resulting pattern challenges the assumption that spending more inference computation on a single reasoning trace reliably produces better results.

To explain this pattern, the authors introduce a simple probabilistic model. In their analysis, additional thinking increases variation in outputs, and the interaction between uncertainty and the evaluation metric can make that variation appear beneficial. They interpret the observed early gains as an unreliable indication of improved reasoning, with longer continuation eventually reducing precision through overthinking.

Their alternative is parallel thinking: generate several independent reasoning paths within the same inference budget and select the answer receiving the most votes. This approach achieves up to 20% higher accuracy than extended thinking in the reported evaluation. The findings favor spending the tested budget on independent attempts and agreement rather than continually extending one attempt.
neurips-2025-does-thinking-more-always-h.tldr: Extended reasoning eventually hurts performance in the studied settings, while independent reasoning paths with majority voting use the same budget more effectively.

paragraphs: Online optimization evaluates decisions made over time against a benchmark. Dynamic regret allows that benchmark to change at every step, making it useful for studying adaptation. This paper observes that an entire changing benchmark sequence can also be viewed as one fixed function that maps time to a benchmark decision.

The authors use this observation to turn dynamic regret into static regret in a carefully constructed reproducing kernel Hilbert space. For linear losses, the reduction recovers an optimal guarantee governed by the benchmark’s total movement and the time horizon. It also produces new guarantees that adapt to scale and direction, expanding what this reduction can establish.

Unlike earlier dynamic-to-static reductions restricted to linear losses, the proposed reduction applies to any loss sequence. When losses have meaningful curvature, it yields bounds involving the comparator function’s norm and the function space’s effective dimension. Although the construction uses an infinite-dimensional space, its reproducing property makes the resulting algorithms computable. The contribution connects changing benchmarks to established tools for competing against a fixed object.
neurips-2025-dynamic-regret-reduces-to-k.tldr: Viewing a changing benchmark as a fixed function converts dynamic regret into kernelized static regret and yields broader adaptive guarantees.

paragraphs: Graph neural networks often need to produce outputs that obey constraints determined by their inputs. This is difficult when different graphs require outputs of different sizes. ProjNet addresses that setting by incorporating constraint enforcement into a graph neural network framework, so feasibility is part of how its outputs are produced.

The framework combines sparse vector clipping with Component-Averaged Dykstra, an iterative algorithm for finding a best approximation subject to constraints. The authors establish a convergence result for this algorithm and implement it on GPUs to handle large inputs efficiently. For end-to-end training, they introduce a surrogate gradient that is cheaper to compute and better suited to optimization than the exact gradient.

Evaluation spans linear programming, two classes of non-convex quadratic programs, and radio transmit power optimization. These experiments demonstrate effectiveness across several optimization settings. The distinction between constraints and objectives matters here: enforcing convex constraints can still be relevant when the optimization objective is non-convex. ProjNet brings feasibility, scalable computation, and trainability together in one framework.
neurips-2025-enforcing-convex-constraint.tldr: ProjNet integrates convex constraint enforcement into graph neural networks using a scalable iterative algorithm and an efficient training gradient.

paragraphs: This paper learns how to choose actions in classical planning by ranking the actions available at a decision point. The motivation is that a planner needs to identify useful next actions, while learning a value function requires globally consistent evaluations. A ranking policy only needs local consistency among the choices it compares.

The authors introduce a graph representation that explicitly includes action information. A graph neural network augmented with gated recurrent units then learns action rankings from that representation. Training examples come from small planning problems that existing planners can solve easily. The resulting policy is applied to substantially larger instances where conventional planning becomes computationally prohibitive.

Across standard planning benchmarks, the approach generalizes better to larger problems than those used during training and outperforms multiple value-function and action-ranking baselines in success rate and plan quality. These results support the usefulness of learning relative preferences between actions. They also show that solutions to manageable training instances can provide guidance for harder instances in the evaluated planning settings.
neurips-2025-graph-neural-network-based-.tldr: A graph neural network learns local action rankings from small planning problems and transfers them to larger instances with improved success and plan quality.

paragraphs: ICPC-Eval evaluates language models on difficult programming problems arranged to reflect actual competitive programming contests. It contains 118 curated problems from 11 ICPC contests across different regions. The benchmark preserves contest-like distributions of problem types and difficulty, addressing the authors’ concern that existing coding benchmarks inadequately capture real competition environments.

The work also provides a test-case generation method and a local evaluation toolkit. Its Refine@K metric allows models to repair solutions iteratively using execution feedback. This changes what evaluation can reveal: instead of only measuring whether submitted attempts succeed, it also examines a model’s ability to use feedback to improve its code.

The results show that leading reasoning models, including DeepSeek-R1, often need multiple rounds of code feedback to fully express their in-context reasoning potential relative to non-reasoning models. Even with recent progress, the evaluated models remain behind top human teams. The benchmark therefore combines demanding tasks with an evaluation process that makes iterative correction part of the assessment.
neurips-2025-icpc-eval-probing-the-front.tldr: ICPC-Eval tests contest-level programming and iterative code repair, revealing benefits from execution feedback and a remaining gap to top human teams.

paragraphs: Image as a World turns a single image into a generated panoramic video environment that users can explore through viewpoint rotation and extend over time. The framework separates this process into initialization, exploration, and continuation. Initialization fills out a spatially complete, dynamic scene; exploration changes the viewing direction; continuation advances the generated scene while maintaining temporal consistency.

The visual world model uses generative diffusion models with spherical 3D positional encoding and multi-view composition. These components represent geometry and the meaning of different views within the panoramic scene. A separately fine-tuned vision-language model produces both global and view-specific prompts, helping guide the generated content and improve alignment with the intended scene.

Qualitative and quantitative experiments report superior visual quality, little distortion, and seamless continuation. The authors describe this as, to their knowledge, the first system combining controllability, consistency, and temporal expansion for a 360-degree world generated from one image. Its contribution is the integration of these capabilities into a single pipeline starting from an easily acquired input.
neurips-2025-image-as-a-world-generating.tldr: Image as a World generates controllable 360-degree videos from one image, supporting viewpoint rotation and temporally consistent continuation.

paragraphs: High accuracy on a controlled image dataset does not necessarily show that an AI-image detector will work reliably on images encountered elsewhere. This paper introduces AIGIBench to examine that gap. Its purpose is to test robustness and generalization under conditions that better reflect the variety of generated images and their real-world presentation.

The benchmark covers four questions: whether detectors generalize across image sources, withstand image degradation, benefit from data augmentation, and respond well to preprocessing at test time. It includes 23 fake-image subsets spanning different generation techniques, together with samples collected from social media and AI art platforms. This makes the evaluation broader than testing one familiar source of synthetic images.

Experiments with 11 advanced detectors reveal substantial performance drops on real-world data despite strong reported results in controlled settings. Common augmentations offer limited benefits, and preprocessing has nuanced effects. These findings show why detection cannot be judged from a single accuracy figure and provide a shared framework for developing more dependable methods.
neurips-2025-is-artificial-intelligence-.tldr: AIGIBench finds that strong controlled-test accuracy does not translate into reliable real-world AI-image detection for the 11 detectors evaluated.

paragraphs: LangHOPS identifies objects and their individual parts in images while preserving the hierarchy connecting them. Given candidate categories expressed through an open vocabulary, it jointly detects instances and segments their image regions. This links fine-grained visual recognition to the larger objects those parts belong to, rather than treating every region as an unrelated category.

The framework grounds object–part hierarchies in language space using a multimodal large language model. Its knowledge and reasoning connect concepts at different levels of detail within the parsing pipeline. The method also uses model-driven refinement of part queries. This approach makes language-grounded relationships central to organizing the visual predictions.

Evaluation covers in-domain and cross-dataset instance segmentation, plus zero-shot semantic segmentation. The reported improvements are 5.5% and 4.8% in Average Precision on PartImageNet, and 2.5% in mIOU for unseen ADE20K object parts. Ablation studies support the contributions of both the language-grounded hierarchy and query refinement. Together, the results demonstrate gains across several forms of fine-grained visual understanding.
neurips-2025-langhops-language-grounded-.tldr: LangHOPS uses language-grounded object–part hierarchies to improve open-vocabulary segmentation, including recognition of unseen parts.

paragraphs: Flow matching learns a velocity field that transforms one probability distribution into another. Rectified flow matching seeks to make those transformation paths straighter. This paper investigates how these constructions relate to optimal transport, examining the mathematical relationship between more direct paths and maps that solve a transport optimization problem.

The authors establish invariance properties and derive explicit velocity fields. They also construct and analyze examples involving Gaussian distributions, including dependent Gaussian settings, and Gaussian mixtures. These concrete cases provide a basis for studying when rectified flows connect to optimal transport and for testing broader claims about that connection.

The paper then scrutinizes claims that constraining the velocity field to be a gradient yields optimal transport solutions asymptotically. Its analysis of solution existence finds that the connection needs substantially stronger assumptions than previously acknowledged. Counterexamples invalidate earlier equivalence results. The conclusion is qualified but consequential: imposing a gradient constraint on rectified flows is generally not a reliable way to compute optimal transport maps.
neurips-2025-on-the-relation-between-rec.tldr: The paper shows that gradient-constrained rectified flows require stronger assumptions to connect to optimal transport than earlier equivalence claims suggested.

paragraphs: Video super-resolution must recover convincing detail while keeping that detail consistent between frames. This paper argues that a pretrained diffusion model needs to preserve reliable temporal information from the degraded input while adding spatial detail. DLoRAL addresses these two requirements through separate but coordinated LoRA training branches.

A Cross-Frame Retrieval module first gathers complementary information across frames, and Consistency-LoRA learns temporal representations robust to degradation. During the detail-learning phase, those components are fixed while Detail-LoRA improves spatial appearance within the temporal representation established by Consistency-LoRA. Alternating the two phases lets the model refine both capabilities while keeping their objectives connected.

At inference, the two LoRA branches are merged into the stable diffusion model, which restores video in one diffusion step. The reported experiments show strong accuracy and speed while producing detailed, temporally coherent outputs. The approach matters because it explicitly organizes adaptation around the tension between frame quality and consistency, then combines the learned adaptations for efficient restoration.
neurips-2025-one-step-diffusion-for-deta.tldr: DLoRAL coordinates separate consistency and detail adaptations to restore detailed, temporally coherent video in one diffusion step.

paragraphs: PLANA3R reconstructs indoor scenes from two images without requiring their camera poses as inputs. It represents geometry using a sparse collection of planar 3D primitives, drawing on the geometric regularities of man-made environments. The framework estimates both metric scene structure and the relative pose of the cameras in a feed-forward process.

Vision Transformers extract the planar primitives, and planar splatting renders them into high-resolution depth and surface-normal maps. Training signals pass through those rendered maps to improve the geometry. Crucially, the method does not need explicit 3D plane annotations: it learns planar structure using depth and normal supervision, supporting training on large stereo datasets.

Tests across indoor datasets show strong generalization to out-of-domain indoor environments for surface reconstruction, depth estimation, and relative pose estimation under metric evaluation. The planar representation also supports accurate plane segmentation. The contribution combines a compact geometric representation with supervision that teaches plane structure indirectly, while retaining usefulness across several related reconstruction tasks.
neurips-2025-plana3r-zero-shot-metric-pl.tldr: PLANA3R learns compact planar indoor reconstructions from two unposed images using depth and normal supervision instead of explicit plane labels.

paragraphs: Reward functions guide what a control policy learns, but designing effective dense rewards often requires expert judgment. Existing language-model approaches generate rewards from task descriptions and revise them using training feedback. This paper identifies two weaknesses in that process: inefficient search and insufficient use of information gathered during earlier attempts.

RF-Agent treats reward design as a sequence of decisions made by a language agent. It integrates Monte Carlo Tree Search to organize the design and optimization process, using the language model’s contextual reasoning across multiple stages. Historical feedback becomes part of the reasoning used to identify promising reward functions, rather than simply prompting another isolated revision.

The authors evaluate the framework on 17 diverse low-level control tasks and report strong results supporting its effectiveness. The main contribution is therefore a structured search process around language-model reward generation. By connecting successive design decisions with accumulated feedback, RF-Agent aims to make reward optimization more efficient and better suited to complex control tasks.
neurips-2025-rf-agent-automated-reward-f.tldr: RF-Agent combines language-model reasoning with Monte Carlo Tree Search to use historical feedback more effectively when designing control rewards.

paragraphs: This work scales reinforcement learning for vision-language models that answer questions about long videos. It combines a dataset, a training procedure, and specialized infrastructure. LongVideo-Reason supplies 104,000 video question–answer pairs with reasoning annotations across domains including sports, games, and vlogs. Training begins with supervised reasoning examples and then applies reinforcement learning.

The infrastructure, Multi-modal Reinforcement Sequence Parallelism, distributes sequence processing and uses a vLLM-based engine tailored to long videos. Cached video embeddings make rollout and prefilling more efficient. The system reports up to a 2.1-fold training speedup and supports reinforcement learning on hour-long videos containing 3,600 frames on a single node with eight A100 GPUs.

The resulting LongVILA-R1-7B model reaches 65.1% VideoMME accuracy without subtitles and 71.1% with them, consistently outperforming LongVILA-7B across multiple benchmarks. It can process up to 8,192 frames with configurable sampling rates. The results connect improvements in reasoning performance with the practical infrastructure needed to train on much longer visual sequences.
neurips-2025-scaling-rl-to-long-videos-9.tldr: A coordinated dataset, training pipeline, and parallel infrastructure improve long-video reasoning while making reinforcement learning on long sequences more practical.

paragraphs: Long reasoning traces are slow to generate token by token. Speculative decoding accelerates generation with drafts, but longer drafts become increasingly unlikely to match the target model exactly. This paper adds another level of parallelism by exploiting the structure of reasoning steps, where semantic correctness can matter more than identical wording.

In lookahead reasoning, a lightweight model proposes several future reasoning steps. The target model expands those proposals in a single batch, and a verifier retains semantically correct steps while the target regenerates rejected ones. Token-level speculative decoding continues inside each step, allowing the step-level and token-level acceleration mechanisms to work together.

The authors show theoretically and empirically that this raises speculative decoding’s peak speedup. Across GSM8K, AIME, and other benchmarks, the reported speedup improves from 1.4-fold to 2.1-fold while preserving answer quality. It also scales better with additional GPU throughput. The key contribution is a way to spend parallel computation on future reasoning steps without demanding exact token agreement across an entire long draft.
neurips-2025-scaling-speculative-decodin.tldr: Lookahead reasoning adds semantic step-level parallelism to speculative decoding, increasing reported speedup from 1.4× to 2.1× while preserving answer quality.

paragraphs: SmartCache targets duplicated computation and memory use when different conversations ask semantically similar questions. Reusing an answer requires matching the conversational context as well as the current query. The system organizes turns in a Semantic Forest, a hierarchical index that supports retrieval under both conditions.

The framework uses attention scores already computed during standard prefill to detect topic changes with little additional overhead. It connects this semantic processing to memory management through a two-level mapping that shares key-value caches across equivalent conversational states. A semantics-aware eviction policy then decides what cached information to retain, linking answer reuse with GPU memory efficiency.

On CoQA and SQuAD, SmartCache reports memory reductions of up to 59.1% against prefix caching and 56.0% against semantic caching, with time-to-first-token reductions of 78.0% and 71.7%, respectively. It also reports answer-quality improvements for Qwen-2.5-1.5B on CoQA. These results show the benefit of jointly considering conversational meaning and low-level cache management instead of treating them as separate optimization problems.
neurips-2025-smartcache-context-aware-se.tldr: SmartCache matches queries together with conversational context to reuse responses and share KV memory, reducing latency and memory use in the reported evaluations.

paragraphs: TabDPT addresses the difficulty of building a foundation model for tables drawn from many different domains. Its approach combines retrieval for in-context learning with self-supervised pretraining. In-context learning lets the model adapt to a new task using examples supplied in context, without requiring an additional round of parameter tuning.

A central investigation compares real and synthetic pretraining data. The authors find that real datasets contain useful signals that synthetic training does not easily capture. Incorporating real data can substantially accelerate training and improve generalization to unseen datasets. This makes the composition of pretraining data an important part of the proposed approach.

The resulting model performs strongly on the CTR23 regression and CC18 classification benchmarks. With the proposed pretraining procedure, increasing both model size and data size produces consistent improvements following power-law trends. These observed scaling relationships suggest a path toward larger tabular foundation models. The contribution joins a practical adaptation strategy with evidence that real-data pretraining and increased scale can improve transfer across tables.
neurips-2025-tabdpt-scaling-tabular-foun.tldr: TabDPT combines retrieval-based in-context learning with real-data pretraining, showing stronger generalization and consistent gains as model and data sizes grow.

paragraphs: This paper studies time-series generation when only a few examples are available for a target setting. A large-scale evaluation finds a substantial gap between leading generative models trained with full datasets and those operating under limited supervision. The proposed response is a unified diffusion model pretrained across a large, heterogeneous collection of time-series datasets.

Pretraining is intended to capture temporal representations that transfer across domains. Dynamic convolutional layers let the architecture adapt flexibly to different channel configurations, while dataset tokens condition generation on the domain. These components allow one framework to accommodate varied time-series datasets while drawing on shared knowledge learned during pretraining.

The model achieves state-of-the-art few-shot results in the reported evaluations, outperforming domain-specific baselines across a range of subset sizes. It also exceeds all evaluated baselines on full-dataset benchmarks. The findings support cross-domain pretraining as a useful foundation for generation with scarce target examples. The small-example claim concerns adaptation to the target setting, alongside substantial pretraining on other time-series data.
neurips-2025-time-series-generation-unde.tldr: A diffusion model pretrained across diverse time series generates strong few-shot results and also outperforms evaluated baselines on full-dataset benchmarks.

paragraphs: Pointing and showing help people communicate what they mean, but interpreting these gestures requires identifying their intended targets. This paper introduces GestureTarget, a task for evaluating that ability in social scenes. The focus is the meaning of a gesture in context: which scene element the person intends to indicate.

The authors propose TransGesture, a family of Transformer-based models. Each receives an image and the location of a person, then predicts the gesture’s intended target within the scene. A gaze-aware version combines gesture information with gaze-following cues through joint cross attention. This lets information about where the person looks contribute to interpreting what their gesture refers to.

The gaze-aware model improves target-mask intersection-over-union by 6% and gesture-existence prediction accuracy by 10%, as reported in the abstract. These results support combining gaze and gesture cues for this task. The work contributes both an evaluation setting and models that make the relationship between visual social signals and intended targets directly measurable.
neurips-2025-toward-human-deictic-gestur.tldr: GestureTarget and TransGesture study what people point or gesture toward, showing that gaze cues improve target localization and gesture detection.

paragraphs: Model merging combines several task-specific experts into one model, but the combined model can lose performance. This paper observes a close correlation between that loss and feature drift: changes in the internal representations produced for the same input after merging. That observation motivates preserving representations more directly during consolidation.

Layer-wise Optimal Task Vector Merging minimizes feature drift between the experts and the merged model one layer at a time. The authors formulate this as a convex quadratic optimization problem and derive closed-form parameter solutions for linear and normalization layers. This allows merging through basic matrix operations, addressing the cost associated with approaches that require secondary training.

Experiments on vision and vision-language benchmarks show substantial improvements over baseline merging methods, including gains of up to 4.4% for ViT-B/32 over state-of-the-art approaches. The contribution is an efficient optimization target tied to the model’s internal behavior. The observed correlation motivates the design, while the experiments provide evidence that reducing drift improves merging in the evaluated settings.
neurips-2025-towards-minimizing-feature-.tldr: LOT Merging combines task experts by analytically minimizing layer-wise feature drift, improving benchmark performance with basic matrix operations.

paragraphs: Protein graph models commonly represent spatial relationships between individual residues. This paper addresses the difficulty of learning both local structure and longer-range relationships efficiently at that level. It introduces a hierarchy built around secondary-structure motifs, including alpha helices, beta strands, and loops, so the representation explicitly contains multiple structural scales.

Each motif becomes a fine-grained subgraph, while a coarse graph connects motifs according to their spatial arrangement and relative orientation. One graph neural network learns interactions within motifs; another learns relationships across motifs. The framework is modular, allowing different graph neural networks to be chosen for either stage rather than requiring one particular architecture.

The authors theoretically show that the hierarchy preserves the desired maximal expressiveness, supporting their claim that the construction retains critical structural information. Experiments show that placing baseline graph networks inside this framework improves prediction accuracy and lowers computational cost across benchmarks. The results support using protein structure itself to organize computation at both local and larger scales.
neurips-2025-towards-multiscale-graph-ba.tldr: A hierarchy of protein motifs and residue-level subgraphs improves graph-model accuracy and efficiency while preserving the framework’s desired expressiveness.

paragraphs: VAGEN trains vision-language agents to reason explicitly about their current situation and what will happen next. Visual observations provide only partial information about the environment, so the work models interaction as a partially observable decision process. It structures reasoning into state estimation and transition modeling, studying five reasoning strategies to establish the importance of this organization.

The study finds that useful internal representations depend on the task. Natural language works well for semantic relationships in general tasks, while structured formats are important for precise manipulation. Training combines a WorldModeling Reward for turn-by-turn state predictions with Bi-Level General Advantage Estimation, which assigns training credit in a way that accounts for interaction turns.

Across five agent tasks, the trained 3B model reaches a reported performance of 0.82, compared with 0.21 before training and 0.75, 0.67, and 0.62 for the listed proprietary reasoning models. These comparisons support the approach within the evaluated tasks. The contribution links explicit state reasoning, task-appropriate representations, and reinforcement-learning feedback in a scalable multi-turn training framework.
neurips-2025-vagen-reinforcing-world-mod.tldr: VAGEN rewards explicit state estimation and transition prediction, substantially improving a 3B visual agent across five evaluated tasks.

paragraphs: VisualLens explores whether images from everyday life can support personalized recommendations without relying on a history specific to the recommendation task. The motivating hypothesis is that a person’s visual history contains clues about interests and preferences that can transfer across contexts. This addresses situations where item-based interaction histories are unavailable or difficult to generalize.

The framework uses multimodal large language models to extract, filter, and refine a user profile from those images. That profile then supports recommendation. The authors also introduce Google-Review-V and Yelp-V, two benchmarks containing task-agnostic visual histories, so the proposed source of personalization can be evaluated directly.

On these benchmarks, VisualLens improves Hit@3 by a reported 5–10% over state-of-the-art item-based multimodal recommendation methods and outperforms GPT-4o by 2–5%. Further analysis finds robustness across different history lengths and strong adaptation to longer histories and unseen content categories. The findings support visual history as a useful source of transferable preference information in the studied recommendation settings.
neurips-2025-visuallens-personalization-.tldr: VisualLens builds preference profiles from everyday images, improving recommendations on two benchmarks without requiring task-specific visual histories.
